sections.title: Section 1
sections.context: A book club organiser books group theatre tickets by phone

transcript.text: Good morning, Regency Theatre box office, Sam speaking.
Oh, hello. I'd like to book a block of seats for The Glass Orchard, please. I run a book club and there are quite a few of us coming.
Lovely — that one's selling fast. Can I take your surname first?
It's Pallister.
Is that P-A-L-I-S-T-E-R?
Nearly — there's a double L in the middle. P-A-double L-I-S-T-E-R.
P-A-L-L-I-S-T-E-R, got it. And a daytime phone number?
My mobile: oh-seven-eight-double-one, four-oh-two, five-six-three.
Four-oh-two, six-five-three—
No, sorry — five-six-three. Five, six, three.
Five-six-three, my mistake. Right, which performance were you hoping for?
The Friday evening — that's the seventeenth of October.
Ah. The seventeenth sold out last week, I'm afraid — the reviews have been very kind to us. But I've got good availability for Saturday the eighteenth, the evening show at seven thirty.
Saturday the eighteenth... let me think... yes, that should suit most of us. Let's book that.
And how many in the group?
Twelve. It was going to be fourteen, but two people have dropped out.
Twelve it is. Now, seating. Stalls are thirty pounds, the circle is twenty-five, and the balcony is sixteen.
Ooh, the balcony's tempting at that price...
I should be honest with you — the front rows of the balcony have a safety rail running right across the view. That's why they're cheap. For a special night out, I really wouldn't.
No, nobody wants to spend the evening peering round a rail. We'll take the circle, then.
Circle, twelve seats together. Now, since it's a group — do you know about our discount scheme?
I read on your website that it's ten per cent for groups of eight or more?

That page is out of date, I'm afraid — the website's being rebuilt. The current scheme is actually fifteen per cent, but it starts at ten people rather than eight. With twelve of you, you qualify comfortably.
Even better. So what does that come to?
Twelve seats at twenty-five is three hundred pounds; take off fifteen per cent, that's forty-five off — so two hundred and fifty-five pounds altogether.
Two fifty-five. Fine.

And one thing you might enjoy: on the Saturday there's a free pre-show talk with the director. It starts at quarter to seven and it's held in the studio — that's the smaller space to the left of the main foyer. Lasts about half an hour. I can reserve talk places for your group at no charge.
Oh, the club would love that — yes, add all twelve of us, please.

Done. Last thing — tickets. We don't post them out any more. They'll be waiting at the box office window from an hour before the show, and whoever collects them just needs to quote the booking reference. I'll text that reference to the mobile number you gave me.
The booking reference — not a bank card?
The reference on its own is fine. I'll send you a secure payment link today, and once that's paid you're all set.
Wonderful. Thanks so much, Sam.
A pleasure. Enjoy the show on the eighteenth, Ms Pallister.

sections.title: Section 2
sections.context: A sports centre manager gives new students an orientation talk

transcript.text: Morning, everyone, and welcome to the university sports centre. I'm Gareth, the centre manager, and in the next few minutes I'll point you round the site, flag one temporary problem, and explain how booking works this year — because it's changed.

First, the geography. You all came in through the main entrance on College Road, and the footpath runs north from there right through the middle of the site. The membership desk is just inside that main entrance — cards, queries, lost property, all handled there.

Walking up the path, on your left opposite the car park you'll see the outdoor gym — a dozen weatherproof machines, free to use, no booking needed. The main sports hall is the big grey building further along on the right, and the fitness suite — that's the indoor gym, treadmills, weights, the serious toys — is in the basement of the sports hall. Take the stairs down by the hall's front doors.

Right at the far north end of the site, behind the tennis courts, is the new climbing wall. Twelve metres, forty routes, and yes, all the equipment's provided. On the east side of the site, beside the lake, there's the boathouse — the rowing and kayaking clubs live there, and beginners' taster sessions run every Saturday morning in term time.

One more spot worth knowing: the physiotherapy clinic sits between the sports hall and the running track. Students get a discounted rate, and honestly, see them early — a niggle in week two is cheaper than an injury in week ten.

Now, the bad news, and I'd rather you heard it from me. The swimming pool closes from this Monday for two weeks while we replace the entire filtration system. It's twenty years old and it owes us nothing. The pool reopens on the ninth of October. In the meantime we've arranged free swimming for all members at the Riverside pool in town — normally four pounds fifty a visit, but free for you; just show your campus card at their reception.

Next, fitness classes — yoga, spinning, circuits, all of it. In previous years you had to queue at the reception desk at eight in the morning to sign up, and frankly it was chaos, people were queuing in their pyjamas. From this term, registration has moved online. You go to the sports centre website, log in with your student number, and bookings open at six each evening for the following day. No more queues, no more pyjamas.

A quick word on money, because I get asked every year. Your membership includes the gym induction — that's the one-hour session where we show you the machines, and you can't use the fitness suite until you've done it, so book it this week. Classes are extra, three pounds each, and towel hire is a pound. The induction, though — completely free.
Last thing: lockers. Bring your own padlock, don't leave anything overnight, and anything that is left overnight ends up at the membership desk looking embarrassed. Right — questions, anyone?

sections.title: Section 3
sections.context: Two students and their tutor plan a short documentary assignment

transcript.text: Come in, both of you. So — the five-minute documentary. Have you settled on a subject yet?
We had two on the shortlist: the university bee project, and the night market on Canal Street.

And we've gone for the night market. The bee project is worthy, but visually it's... hives in a field. The market gives us lanterns, steam, crowds, faces — it's a far stronger film before anyone says a word.
I agree, for once. You can't light a beehive.
Good — pick the subject your camera loves, not the one your conscience does. Now, interviews. Who's on your list?
My first thought was the market's publicity manager. I emailed her and she offered straight away.
And that's exactly what worried me. Anything she says will sound like an advert — rehearsed lines about a vibrant community hub.
I'm with Zoe on this one. Publicity people give you polished answers, and polish is dull on film. Who would you use instead?
The stallholders themselves. There's a woman who's run the same noodle stand for twenty years — she remembers when the whole street was warehouses. That's your history.
Fair enough. The manager's out, the stallholders are in.
Now the practical side, and this matters: you're filming on a public street, so you'll need a filming permit from the city council. Anything with a tripod counts as filming, in their eyes.

I looked into that yesterday. The good news is it's free for students. The catch is the processing time — it takes ten days... sorry, ten working days, so realistically two full weeks. I'll submit the form tomorrow morning.

Do. And one suggestion from me: don't just film the market in full swing. Get there in the late afternoon and film the setting-up — empty street, stalls going up, lights coming on one by one. That transformation could open the whole film.
Oh, that's much better than opening on crowd shots. We'll do that.
Can I raise one more idea? My cousin has a drone. Aerial shots of the whole market at night would look incredible—
Marcus, no. A drone over a crowded street at night? That needs a separate licence, and the buzzing would wreck every piece of audio we record.
Zoe's right, I'm afraid. Flying over crowds is illegal without an operator's certificate, and none of you holds one. Keep the camera on the ground.
All right, all right — the drone stays at home. It would have looked great, though.

Now, deadlines, and you won't like this. You'll have seen my email — the screening room is being rewired in the last week of November, so I've had to bring the rough cut forward. It was due on the twenty-eighth; it's now due on the twenty-first of November.
A whole week less. That's tight with two market shoots.
It is, which is why I've booked the editing suite for you every Wednesday between now and then. Use it — don't leave the edit for the final weekend.
Wednesdays in the editing suite, rough cut on the twenty-first. One last thing from me: the market's loud, so whatever we record, I think we subtitle all the interviews.
Sensible. Plan for subtitles now and you won't be rescuing sound at midnight later. Right — permit form tomorrow, and I'll see you both on Wednesday.

questions.explain: Zoe's reason is visual: lanterns, steam, crowds versus 'hives in a field' — the rejected bee project is the built-in distractor; access and other groups are never mentioned.

questions.explain: She actually 'offered straight away' — the opposite of refusing; the problem is that 'anything she says will sound like an advert — rehearsed lines', so willingness is the trap in A.

questions.explain: A disagreement resolved: Marcus proposes it, Zoe and the tutor object (licence, noise, illegality over crowds), and Marcus concedes — 'the drone stays at home'.

sections.title: Section 4
sections.context: A lecture on playground design and its effects on child development

transcript.text: Today's lecture is about playgrounds — what forty years of safety-driven design has actually done to children, and why the research now points somewhere uncomfortable.

Let me begin with a distinction the whole field rests on. A risk is a challenge that a child can recognise and choose for themselves — a high ladder, a fast slide, a wobbly log. The child sees it, weighs it, and decides. A danger that a child cannot see for themselves is called a hazard — a rotten plank, a rusted bolt, broken glass under the sand. The two deserve opposite treatments: hazards should be removed ruthlessly, but risk, the research suggests, is something children actually need.

From the nineteen-eighties onwards, though, driven partly by lawsuits, playgrounds across the developed world were systematically flattened. Equipment got lower and slower, and beneath it, councils installed rubber surfacing — that springy, brightly coloured ground you now see everywhere. The assumption was straightforward: softer landings and lower platforms would mean fewer injuries.

Here is the paradox: injury rates barely moved. Study after study found the totals stubbornly flat, and to understand why, watch the children rather than the equipment. A bored child does not stop taking risks; a bored child goes looking for extra stimulation — climbing onto the roof of the low slide, using equipment in ways no designer intended. Take the challenge out of the playground and children simply reintroduce it themselves.

And the popular explanation for playground injuries turns out to be wrong as well. Ask the public and they will blame falls from high equipment. But when researchers actually analysed accident records, most playground injuries happen when children are running on level ground — collisions, trips, twisted ankles — not falling from height at all.

So what does better look like? One answer arrived from an unexpected direction: junk. Several schools began providing movable materials with no fixed purpose — tyres, planks, crates, ropes — known in the literature as loose parts. Children combine them, negotiate over them, build and rebuild with them. In trials where schools introduced loose parts at playtime, staff recorded children playing for longer, and noticeably more cooperation between children, because a plank across two crates is a bridge only if somebody agrees to hold it steady.

Regulation has begun to catch up. Many councils have replaced the standard safety checklist with what's called risk-benefit assessment: instead of asking only 'what could go wrong here?', assessors weigh the dangers of a feature against the developmental gains it offers. A climbing boulder might bruise a knee; it also teaches grip, judgement and nerve — and under risk-benefit assessment, it usually passes.

Does any of this show up in the children themselves? The observation studies say yes, with the usual caveats about sample sizes. Children in more challenging playgrounds are, in most studies, more physically active across the whole day, not just at playtime. And adventurous play is consistently linked with gains in balance and, more strikingly, in confidence — children trusted with manageable risk become more willing to attempt new tasks of every kind.

Designers now put the goal in a single sentence, and it's the one I'd like you to leave with. A good playground should be as safe as necessary — not as safe as possible. Remove every hazard; keep the risk. Next week, we'll look at how the same thinking is reshaping school sports.

questions.explain: The cause-and-effect link: 'a bored child goes looking for extra stimulation', reintroducing the removed challenge in less supervised ways.

questions.prompt: Most playground injuries actually occur while children are ______ on level ground.
questions.explain: This corrects the popular explanation: the public blames falls from height, but accident records show most injuries 'happen when children are running on level ground'.

questions.prompt: Movable materials such as tyres, planks and crates are known as ______.
questions.explain: The second defined term: materials 'with no fixed purpose... known in the literature as loose parts'.

questions.prompt: With loose parts, staff observed longer play and more ______ between children.
questions.explain: 'Staff recorded children playing for longer, and... noticeably more cooperation between children.'

questions.prompt: Many councils now use ______ assessment in place of the old safety checklist.
questions.explain: 'Many councils have replaced the standard safety checklist with what's called risk-benefit assessment', weighing dangers against developmental gains.

questions.prompt: In most studies, children in challenging playgrounds are more physically ______ all day.
questions.explain: A qualified claim — 'in most studies' — that such children are 'more physically active across the whole day, not just at playtime'.

questions.prompt: Adventurous play is linked with improvements in balance and in ______.
questions.explain: 'Adventurous play is consistently linked with gains in balance and, more strikingly, in confidence.'

questions.prompt: A good playground should be 'as safe as ______', not as safe as possible.
questions.explain: The closing principle: 'as safe as necessary — not as safe as possible. Remove every hazard; keep the risk.' 'Possible' is the deliberately contrasted distractor.
